sub_sections.title: Quality and pertinence of the project's research and innovation objectives (and the extent to which they are ambitious, and go beyond the state of the art)
sub_sections.content:
# 1.1 Quality and pertinence of the project's research and innovation objectives (and the extent to which they are ambitious, and go beyond the state of the art)

## 1.1.1 European challenge and scientific rationale

European agriculture is entering an increasingly water-constrained production environment. Approximately 30% of EU territory is affected by seasonal water scarcity in an average year, while climate change is expected to intensify drought frequency, severity and seasonal fluctuations in freshwater availability. Agriculture is particularly exposed: southern Europe accounts for a large share of EU agricultural water abstraction, and climate change is expected both to increase the agricultural area requiring irrigation and to raise irrigation demand in already irrigated areas. For high-value horticultural field crops, inappropriate irrigation timing degrades productivity, fruit quality, water-use efficiency and economic return. FIELDWISE uses processing tomato as its model crop precisely because it is a demanding system for predictive irrigation, in which productivity depends strongly on the temporal interaction between water availability, atmospheric demand, developmental stage and irrigation management. The central, pertinent question the fellowship addresses is whether developing crop water stress can be identified early enough for irrigation management to prevent or reduce damaging physiological stress. This grounds the project's objectives directly in a recognised European environmental and agronomic problem rather than in a purely methodological curiosity, which is the first test of pertinence for the Excellence criterion (weighted 50% for MSCA-PF).

## 1.1.2 The six research and innovation objectives

FIELDWISE is a single-researcher action carried out by the experienced researcher Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, hosted at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) in Hungary under a European Fellowship of 30 months (a 24-month fellowship at ELTE, M1–M24, plus a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR, M25–M30). Its scientific programme is organised around six research and innovation objectives, each carrying an explicit, verifiable measurable output and each realised by a dedicated work package:

- **O1 — Construct a harmonised five-year MATE soil-plant-atmosphere dataset.** Measurable output: a QC-controlled historical database and documented metadata. Realised in WP1 (Historical Data and Target Design) and evidenced by deliverable D1.1 (Harmonised historical database, due month 6) and D1.2 (Data/target/validation protocol, due month 6).
- **O2 — Identify physiologically meaningful hyperspectral early-warning signatures and establish their Sentinel-2 transferability.** Measurable output: a validated hyperspectral/Sentinel-compatible feature library. Realised in WP2 (Physiological Early Warning and Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel Transfer) and evidenced by D2.1 (Physiological validation dataset, due month 14) and D2.2 (Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library, due month 14).
- **O3 — Develop prospective uncertainty-aware crop water-stress forecasts.** Measurable output: calibrated forecasts at actionable horizons. Realised in WP3 (Prospective and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction) and evidenced by D3.1 (Comparative modelling benchmark, due month 18) and D3.2 (FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card, due month 18).
- **O4 — Quantify temporal and Hungary->Bulgaria geographic transferability and evaluate adaptation.** Measurable output: an independent transferability benchmark. Realised in WP4 (Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability) and evidenced by D4.1 (Temporal transferability benchmark, due month 21), D4.2 (Hungary->Bulgaria transferability report, due month 21) and D4.3 (Adaptation protocol, due month 21).
- **O5 — Quantify research->commercial-field operational transferability.** Measurable output: an AgroVIR farmer-field evaluation. Realised in WP5 (Operational Transfer, Decision Value and Web MVP) and evidenced by D5.2 (Commercial-field transferability assessment, due month 30) and D5.4 (AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation, due month 30).
- **O6 — Translate validated predictions into irrigation priority and a functional web MVP.** Measurable output: a DrR web MVP + Field Decision Value + AgroVIR requirements assessment. Realised in WP5 and evidenced by D5.1 (DrR web MVP, due month 24), D5.3 (Field Decision Value report, due month 30) and D5.5 (FMIS integration roadmap, due month 30).

The objectives are deliberately sequential and mutually dependent rather than parallel and independent: O1 supplies the harmonised evidence base on which O2 discovers physiological signatures; O2's feature library feeds the prospective models of O3; O3's calibrated engine is the object whose robustness O4 stress-tests across seasons and across the Hungary-to-Bulgaria boundary; and O5–O6 carry the surviving model into commercial conditions and into an operational decision tool. This chain reflects the project's core logic — a signal is only valuable if it survives the whole journey from plant physiology to satellite observation, from Hungary to Bulgaria, and from experimental fields to farming reality, while arriving early enough to change the irrigation decision.

## 1.1.3 Measurability, verifiability and realistic achievability

Each objective is stated with a concrete, inspectable measurable output (listed above) rather than an aspiration, and each output is bound to one or more named deliverables in the work-package structure with defined due months. This makes the objectives verifiable at defined points in the timeline: an evaluator can check O1 against the harmonised database and protocol at month 6, O2 against the feature library at month 14, O3 against the comparative benchmark and model card at month 18, O4 against the temporal and cross-country reports at month 21, and O5–O6 against the DrR web MVP at month 24 and the commercial-field, decision-value, AgroVIR-evaluation and FMIS-roadmap outputs at month 30. The measurability extends below the objective level: the concept fixes seven research questions (RQ1–RQ7) and six falsifiable hypotheses (H1–H6), so that each objective is discharged not merely by producing an artefact but by returning an evidenced answer. For example, H3 predicts that performance on an unseen season will be lower than under conventional random validation, and H4 predicts a measurable geographic performance drop from MATE, Hungary to MVCRI, Bulgaria that limited local calibration partially recovers — both are quantitative, testable claims whose confirmation or refutation is itself the result. This design directly answers the previous evaluation's criticism, recorded in the strategic positioning, that milestones occurred too late to enable corrective action: WP1 establishes a leakage-safe validation design before any predictive claim is made, so honest, non-optimistic performance estimates are available at each transfer step.

Realistic achievability rests on four grounded factors. First, the project does not start from a blank technology base: the researcher has already initiated DrR - Digital Agronomist, a desktop research prototype that demonstrates the technical feasibility of integrating soil-sensor information, field meteorological-station observations and Sentinel-2A data within a common digital environment; FIELDWISE supplies the missing scientific validation and transferability framework rather than a first build. Second, the primary evidence base already exists — an approximately five-year MATE hyperspectral, soil and meteorological archive — so the data-intensive O1 reuses existing observations instead of depending on a speculative new measurement campaign. Third, the geographic transferability test is anchored in a real cross-country environment at the Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute (MVCRI) in Bulgaria and the operational test in a real commercial evaluator, AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság, which hosts the non-academic placement. Fourth, the objectives are scoped honestly: the web MVP is presented as the research-to-operation demonstrator and not as the primary scientific objective, and full commercial FMIS integration is explicitly deferred to a named post-MSCA route rather than promised within the fellowship. The scale — one experienced researcher over 30 months, supervised at ELTE by Prof. András Jung with Dr. Roland Hollós as methodological co-supervisor for model development and testing — is matched to a staged programme in which each work package hands a defined, quality-assured input to the next.

## 1.1.4 Ambition and advance beyond the state of the art

The ambition of FIELDWISE is expressed as a fundamental reorientation of agricultural AI: from retrospective accuracy to prospective prediction, then to transferability, and finally to field-level decision value. The state of the art in agricultural machine learning is predominantly evaluated through retrospective metrics — R², RMSE, F1-score or classification accuracy — which the concept shows to be an insufficient and sometimes misleading basis for irrigation management, because related seasons or plots can leak between training and testing, because models can learn environment-specific relationships rather than transferable crop-water relationships, because accurate identification of an already-established stress condition can arrive too late to change the decision, and because models that transfer between research experiments can still fail under the heterogeneity and incomplete data of commercial farming. Against this baseline, FIELDWISE advances the field through six explicit transitions that structure the ambition and map one-to-one onto the objectives:

1. Spectral proxy -> Physiological target (O1–O2): replacing vegetation-index proxy definitions of stress with physiologically meaningful plant-response targets (addressing gap G1).
2. Hyperspectral discovery -> Satellite scaling (O2): establishing which high-information proximal hyperspectral stress signatures can be translated to Sentinel-2 spectral and spatial resolution (gap G2), a methodological bridge between proximal hyperspectral observation and scalable satellite prediction.
3. Static detection -> Prospective prediction (O3): forecasting future stress with calibrated, uncertainty-aware models at actionable lead times instead of mapping current condition (gap G3).
4. Internal validation -> Temporal transferability (O4): quantifying the true cost of generalising to unseen seasons under leakage-safe design (gap G3/G4).
5. Single-country modelling -> Geographic transferability (O4): an explicit MATE (Hungary) -> MVCRI (Bulgaria) cross-country transfer test with a stated local-calibration cost (gap G4).
6. Research accuracy -> Commercial-field decision value (O5–O6): moving from research-field accuracy to demonstrated usefulness under commercial farming conditions (gaps G5 and G6).

Two elements are genuinely novel relative to standard practice. First, the project introduces Field Decision Value (FDV) as a final evaluation layer, testing hypothesis H6 that the model with the highest retrospective accuracy will not necessarily deliver the greatest irrigation decision value, because warning lead time, calibration and the balance of false and missed interventions also determine usefulness. This reframes model selection around operational usefulness rather than retrospective fit — a shift the state of the art rarely operationalises. Second, the four-step validation ladder — MATE scientific development and validation -> MVCRI cross-country transferability -> AgroVIR farmer-field operational transferability -> DrR Web MVP research-to-operation delivery — subjects a single predictive engine to temporal, geographic and operational transfer in sequence, exposing where locally developed agricultural intelligence stops being reliable. This addresses a wider European question that the state of the art largely leaves untested: how locally developed agricultural AI can become reliably transferable rather than remaining confined to the field in which it was trained. The ambition is therefore high but disciplined — it is the ambition of proving (or honestly bounding) transferability and decision value, not of asserting a headline accuracy number, and it is directly responsive to the prior submission's documented weaknesses on heterogeneous-data treatment and on the economic/technological route to users.

## 1.1.5 Pertinence to the call and to the fellow's training

Because MSCA-PF is a training-through-research action, the objectives are pertinent not only scientifically but developmentally. The interdisciplinary reach of O1–O6 — spanning crop physiology, hyperspectral and Earth-observation science, uncertainty-aware machine learning, cross-country model adaptation and operational decision support — is the vehicle for a two-way transfer of knowledge between the fellow and the host and for the fellow's progression toward a distinctive profile combining biological understanding, scalable geospatial prediction and operational decision support. The Career Development Plan (deliverable D1.3, due month 3) formalises this and is established jointly by the supervisors and the researcher, satisfying the call's Career Development Plan requirement. The objectives thus serve the call's expected outcomes for supported fellows (increased research and transferable skills and new inter-sectoral, interdisciplinary mind-sets) at the same time as they advance the science, which is the intended alignment for this criterion.

sub_sections.title: Soundness of the proposed methodology (including interdisciplinary approaches, consideration of the gender dimension and other diversity aspects if relevant for the research project, and the quality of open science practices)
sub_sections.content:
# 1.2 Soundness of the proposed methodology (including interdisciplinary approaches, consideration of the gender dimension and other diversity aspects if relevant for the research project, and the quality of open science practices)

## 1.2.1 Overall methodology: the concepts, models and assumptions that underpin the work

The methodological core of FIELDWISE is a deliberate reorientation of how an agricultural prediction model is defined, built and judged. The concept that underpins the whole methodology is that operational value in irrigation support is not established by retrospective fit. Agricultural machine learning is predominantly evaluated through retrospective metrics such as R², RMSE, F1-score or classification accuracy, and a model can achieve strong retrospective performance while being unsuitable for irrigation management: observations from related seasons, plots or fields can leak between training and testing and produce optimistic estimates; a model can learn environment-specific relationships tied to a particular soil, cultivar, management regime or year rather than transferable crop-water relationships; accurate identification of an already-established stress condition can arrive too late to change the decision; and a model that transfers between research experiments can still fail under the heterogeneity and incomplete data of commercial farming. The methodology is therefore organised as a staged progression — from retrospective accuracy to prospective prediction, then to transferability, and finally to field-level decision value — and every methodological choice below is subordinate to that progression. This design directly enables the six objectives: it is the mechanism by which O1 through O6 are discharged with evidence rather than assertion.

**Concepts and target definition (enables O1, O2).** The first methodological commitment is to define water stress through physiologically meaningful plant responses rather than solely through vegetation-index proxies, replacing a spectral-proxy definition with a physiologically grounded target. In WP1 (Historical Data and Target Design) the approximately five-year MATE hyperspectral, soil, weather and management archive is harmonised, its missingness and data quality are audited, a physiological stress definition is established, and — critically — a leakage-safe validation design is fixed before any predictive claim is made. This is the concept that governs measurement integrity for the entire project: the validation split manifests are treated as a first-class, versioned methodological artefact, published in D1.2 (Data/target/validation protocol, due month 6) alongside D1.1 (Harmonised historical database, due month 6). WP2 (Physiological Early Warning and Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel Transfer) then discovers hyperspectral stress signatures and establishes which of them can be reproduced or approximated at Sentinel-2 spectral and spatial resolution, using spectral-response-function resampling, concurrent proximal/satellite observation and scale-aware calibration. The methodological output is a validated, Sentinel-compatible feature basis, captured in D2.1 (Physiological validation dataset, due month 14) and D2.2 (Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library, due month 14). This bridge between high-information proximal hyperspectral observation and scalable satellite prediction is one of the two genuinely novel methodological contributions of the action.

**Models (enables O3).** WP3 (Prospective and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction) turns the feature basis into prospective, uncertainty-aware forecasts of future stress at actionable lead times, rather than mapping current condition. The modelling strategy is deliberately laddered from transparent to complex: temporal feature engineering, then transparent baseline models, then random-forest/gradient-boosted (RF/XGBoost) models, then Bayesian and hierarchical models, with explicit multi-horizon forecasting, probability calibration and uncertainty quantification, and feature-ablation and error analysis. The guiding assumption is parsimony: the simplest adequate model is preferred and deeper architectures are introduced only where sample size and temporal density justify them, which is also the project's stated environmental-sustainability posture. The comparative evidence is reported in D3.1 (Comparative modelling benchmark, due month 18) and the released engine is documented in D3.2 (FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card, due month 18).

**Transferability and decision value (enables O4, O5, O6).** The methodology's distinctive feature is that a single predictive engine is then subjected, in sequence, to temporal, geographic and operational transfer. WP4 (Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability) uses leave-one-year-out validation on the MATE archive, independent field/plot validation where possible, zero-shot MATE→MVCRI transfer, a quantified geographic transferability-gap assessment, limited Bulgarian calibration and hierarchical/Bayesian adaptation, and the identification of universal versus site-specific predictors — reported in D4.1 (Temporal transferability benchmark, due month 21), D4.2 (Hungary->Bulgaria transferability report, due month 21) and D4.3 (Adaptation protocol, due month 21). WP5 (Operational Transfer, Decision Value and Web MVP) carries the surviving model into commercial conditions and introduces Field Decision Value (FDV) as the final evaluation layer: FDV computes usefulness — warning lead time, calibration, and the balance of false and missed interventions — for competing models, evidenced in D5.3 (Field Decision Value report, due month 30). The concrete artefacts are the DrR web MVP (D5.1, due month 24), the commercial-field evaluation D5.2 (Commercial-field transferability assessment, due month 30) and D5.4 (AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation, due month 30), and D5.5 (FMIS integration roadmap, due month 30).

**Underpinning assumptions, stated as testable hypotheses.** The methodology does not smuggle its assumptions in as background conditions; it states them as six falsifiable hypotheses and designs the experiments to confirm or refute them. H1 assumes soil-water and atmospheric-demand information combined with hyperspectral crop-response information will identify developing stress before substantial canopy-greenness deterioration; H2 assumes a subset of hyperspectral features can be made Sentinel-compatible through resampling, concurrent observation and scale-aware calibration; H3 assumes unseen-season performance will be lower than under conventional random validation; H4 assumes performance will decrease from MATE, Hungary to MVCRI, Bulgaria, with limited local calibration and/or hierarchical modelling recovering part of the loss; H5 assumes further degradation on transfer from research to farmer-managed fields, revealing which inputs and components are operationally robust; and H6 assumes the model with the highest retrospective accuracy will not necessarily deliver the greatest decision value. The methodological consequence of H3–H5 is a performance-degradation model of transfer: the project expects and quantifies loss at each transfer step rather than assuming portability. This is the assumption base that makes the honest-estimate design coherent.

## 1.2.2 Methodological challenges identified and how they are overcome

The project has identified its principal methodological challenges explicitly and pairs each with a concrete mitigation, so that the risks are treated as design parameters rather than contingencies. Historical MATE information may be incomplete (mitigated by a common-data subset, quality flags and prospective augmentation); a hyperspectral index may have no Sentinel equivalent (retained for physiological discovery but excluded from the operational Sentinel model); spectral-domain mismatch (SRF resampling plus concurrent-sensor comparison) and proximal/satellite spatial mismatch (representative plot/zone aggregation) are addressed at the transfer step; insufficient physiological stress events are countered by targeted temporal sampling across stress gradients; cloud gaps are handled with temporal windows and Sentinel-1 where scientifically useful. The transfer-failure challenges are met head-on: unseen-year, Hungary→Bulgaria and farmer-field performance drops are treated as expected scientific outcomes to be quantified and adapted to (through limited local/Bayesian adaptation and, where necessary, input/model simplification), rather than as failures to be hidden. Two further challenges are structural to the project's thesis: a prediction that is accurate but too late is guarded against by making lead time a primary model-selection criterion; and the risk that a Bayesian approach does not outperform simpler machine learning is resolved by retaining the simpler model when it is superior in calibration or FDV. Crucially, the methodology adopts an explicit risk philosophy: failure of zero-shot transfer is not project failure — establishing that a MATE-trained model cannot reliably transfer to Bulgaria without a defined amount of local calibration is itself a significant scientific finding. This is what makes the leakage-safe, honest-estimate design methodologically sound: because the deliverables carry quantified degradation and a stated adaptation cost, a negative transfer result is still an evidenced, publishable result. This posture directly answers the prior submission's recorded criticism that its methodological treatment of heterogeneous spatial, spectral and temporal information was insufficient, and that milestones occurred too late to enable corrective action; WP1 fixes validation integrity up front so non-optimistic estimates are available at each subsequent transfer step.

## 1.2.3 Integration of methods and disciplines in pursuit of the objectives

An interdisciplinary approach is not optional for FIELDWISE; it is constitutive of the objectives, because the central problem sits precisely at the interface of crop physiology and geospatial data science. The methodology therefore integrates two disciplinary bases that are normally kept apart. From plant science it draws physiological definition of water stress, horticultural crop and plant-protection knowledge, water-stress experimentation, physiological phenotyping and hyperspectral field measurement, together with the biological interpretation of Earth-observation signals; from geoinformatics and data science it draws EO time-series analysis, optical/SAR integration, hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer, spatio-temporal modelling, Bayesian hierarchical modelling, uncertainty quantification, transfer learning/domain adaptation, reproducible geospatial computation and research-software/web deployment. The integration is realised as a genuinely bidirectional, two-way transfer of knowledge between the experienced researcher, Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, whose foundation is in agronomy, plant protection and plant physiology, and the host, Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), whose remote-sensing and geoinformatics competence supplies the geospatial and modelling methods. This is what makes the physiological-target methodology of WP1–WP2 and the modelling methodology of WP3 a single method rather than two adjacent workstreams: the physiological target defines what the geospatial model must predict, and the geospatial-modelling apparatus determines which physiological signatures can be scaled and forecast.

The disciplinary integration is also operationalised through the supervision structure. Methodological responsibility for model development and testing — the machine-learning, Bayesian/hierarchical and meta-modelling methods and the quality assurance of the modelling and validation design — is provided by the co-supervisor, Dr. Roland Hollós, whose expertise is in machine learning and meta-modelling of crop and grassland multi-model outputs and in agro-meteorology, while overall scientific supervision, remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy are provided by the supervisor, Prof. András Jung. The consortium extends the interdisciplinary reach across sectors and countries: MATE supplies the long-term experimental and physiological knowledge and the source-domain dataset; MVCRI supplies the independent Bulgarian research environment for a true cross-country transfer test (Hungary→Bulgaria, not merely a larger sample); and AgroVIR supplies the bridge from research field to farmer field and from research prototype to operational requirements, producing an academic–research–industry knowledge chain. The methods of these disciplines are not simply juxtaposed: the leakage-safe validation design (data science) governs the physiological experiments (plant science), the FDV framework (decision science and agronomy) governs model selection over the statistical models (machine learning), and the operational assessment (agricultural software engineering, delivered through the non-academic placement) determines which scientific inputs survive into practice. This integration is the vehicle for the call's expected outcomes on new interdisciplinary and inter-sectoral mind-sets and on strengthened R&I capacity and knowledge transfer among participating organisations.

## 1.2.4 Gender dimension and other diversity aspects in the research content

Consistent with the instruction that this question concerns the content of the research and innovation rather than gender balance in the team, the gender dimension has been assessed against the two distinct layers of the methodology. The core scientific object of FIELDWISE is a biophysical system — the water-stress physiology of processing tomato and its interaction with soil water, atmospheric demand, developmental stage and irrigation management, observed through hyperspectral, soil and meteorological data and Sentinel-2. Sex and gender are not explanatory variables for these crop-water and spectral processes, so a sex/gender dimension is not relevant to the biophysical target definition, the hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer, the forecasting models or the temporal and geographic transferability tests. This is the justification the evaluation framework permits where a gender dimension is genuinely not applicable to the research content, and it is stated deliberately rather than by omission.

A gender and diversity dimension does, however, become pertinent at the user-facing layer of the methodology, and the project treats it there. WP5 delivers the DrR web MVP as a decision-support tool for human end-users and includes requirements engineering and user testing with commercial growers together with structured feedback from AgroVIR staff and participating farmers. Because these activities engage human participants (assessed as low-risk in the project's ethics self-assessment, under informed consent with a right of withdrawal and with no special-category data collected), the usability and requirements methodology will consider the diversity of the end-user population — so that the interface, the way stress probability, uncertainty and irrigation priority are communicated, and the operational assumptions are designed for and evaluated with a representative range of users rather than an implicitly homogeneous one; results from human participants are reported only in aggregated or anonymised form. Beyond gender, the research design foregrounds a further diversity axis that is intrinsic to its scientific content: heterogeneity of agro-environments and farming realities. The Hungary-to-Bulgaria transfer test and the research-field-to-commercial-field transfer are, by construction, an examination of whether a model developed in one context remains valid across contrasting soils, cultivars, management regimes and countries — the project's explicit concern with universal versus site-specific predictors is a methodological treatment of environmental and operational diversity, and it is one of the ways the action contributes to the wider European question of how locally developed agricultural intelligence can become reliably transferable.

## 1.2.5 Open science practices as an integral part of the methodology

Open science is embedded in the methodology rather than appended to it, under the governing principle 'as open as possible, as closed as necessary'. The expected open outputs are specified concretely and map onto the methodological artefacts described above: harmonisation protocols and the validation split manifests (the latter being the anti-leakage backbone of the whole approach), the hyperspectral-to-Sentinel methodology, analysis and model code where IP permits, model cards for released models, FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable) metadata, selected derived or anonymised datasets, and open-access publications of the four principal scientific outputs. Two features make these practices load-bearing rather than declarative. First, reproducibility is intrinsic to the scientific claim: because FIELDWISE reports transfer-performance degradation and adaptation cost, the credibility of those numbers depends on publishing the validation design (D1.2, Data/target/validation protocol, due month 6) and the model documentation (the model card in D3.2, due month 18) so that the honest-estimate methodology is externally auditable. Second, open-science competence is trained, not assumed: open science and FAIR practice, research integrity, and generative-AI literacy are named transferable-skill strands of the Career Development Plan (D1.3, due month 3), aligning the action with the call's requirement that training foster an Open Science culture, knowledge valorisation and good scientific conduct including research integrity. The project also observes the necessary closures: farmer yields, irrigation records and field geometries from AgroVIR farms are commercially sensitive and are governed by a data-sharing agreement, so results derived from them are published only in aggregated or anonymised form; personal data in the MVP (user accounts, farm contact details and field boundaries tied to a named holding) are minimised and reviewed by ELTE's Data Protection Officer; and all data remain within the EU. On the specific requirement for a Data Management Plan delivered by month 6: the project commits to a DMP as an integral open-science instrument consistent with this requirement, and its month-6 data-governance artefact in the confirmed work-package structure is D1.2 (Data/target/validation protocol, due month 6), which fixes data harmonisation, quality flags, metadata, the physiological target and the validation design. In candour, the confirmed FIELDWISE deliverable set does not enumerate a separate, standalone 'Data Management Plan' deliverable distinct from D1.2; the DMP is provided here as the standard Horizon Europe/MSCA open-science instrument the action undertakes to deliver by month 6, and this point is flagged rather than presented as an already-scheduled project deliverable, so that the evaluator can see exactly where the confirmed structure ends and the instrument-level commitment begins.

sub_sections.title: Quality of the supervision, training and of the two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host
sub_sections.content:
## 1.3 Quality of the supervision, training and of the two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host

FIELDWISE is a European Fellowship: the experienced researcher Dr. Rositsa Cholakova moves intra-EU from Bulgaria to the host beneficiary, Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) in Hungary, for a 30-month action comprising a 24-month fellowship at ELTE (M1–M24) and a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR (M25–M30). Because it is a European Fellowship, the relevant transfer-of-knowledge test under this criterion is the two-way transfer between the researcher and the host; the three-way transfer required of Global Fellowships (researcher, host, and associated partner for an outgoing phase) does not apply, and no separate secondment is included in this action — the only inter-sectoral mobility is the non-academic placement described in §1.3.4.

## 1.3.1 Qualifications and experience of the supervisory team

Supervision is delivered by a complementary two-person team at the beneficiary, chosen so that the disciplinary reach of the supervision matches the interdisciplinary object of the fellowship — the interface of crop physiology and geospatial data science set out in §1.1 and §1.2. Overall scientific supervision is provided by Prof. András Jung, Professor at ELTE's Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, whose expertise is in remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging, field spectroscopy, geospatial technologies and environmental monitoring. This is precisely the competence base on which the hyperspectral early-warning and hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer methodology of WP2 (Physiological Early Warning and Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel Transfer) depends; it is also directly served by the institute's own hyperspectral instrumentation (the Ultris S5 and Cubert CUVIS Lab Lite in its GIS and Remote Sensing Laboratory). Prof. András Jung chairs the Project Steering Group and is the fellow's primary supervisor and the escalation point for scientific method.

Methodological co-supervision is provided by Dr. Roland Hollós (ORCID 0000-0001-5137-7471) of ELTE's Department of Meteorology, whose expertise is in machine learning and meta-modelling of crop and grassland multi-model outputs and in agro-meteorology. He holds the methodological lead and the quality assurance for model development and testing across WP3 (Prospective and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction) and WP4 (Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability): the fellow designs, builds and runs the models, while the co-supervisor quality-assures the modelling strategy and the leakage-safe validation design that is the backbone of the honest-estimate methodology. His supervision under the action is carried out at the beneficiary, and because the two supervisors sit in different ELTE departments, the supervision is itself interdisciplinary within the host institution — a Bayesian/uncertainty-aware modelling strand alongside the remote-sensing strand. A third, informal scientific-advisory strand is contributed by Prof. Gábor Milics of Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem (MATE), a full professor and Hungary's country representative to the International Society of Precision Agriculture, who advises the fellow personally on remote sensing in precision agriculture (a role he held in the predecessor proposal and continues for FIELDWISE) without occupying a governance seat.

On track record and experience in supervising and training at advanced level, two points are stated with deliberate candour rather than embellishment, consistent with the evaluation framework's status discipline. First, the professorial standing of Prof. András Jung establishes his capacity to supervise at doctoral and postdoctoral level, and the fellow–supervisor pairing is not untested: ELTE hosted a prior MSCA-PF application, PLANTDIGISENSE (HORIZON-MSCA-2025-PF, proposal 101284764), with the same fellow and the same supervisor, which scored 70.40% against a 70.00 threshold. FIELDWISE is therefore a strengthened resubmission by an established pairing that has already worked together on an MSCA-PF proposal at this host, not a first collaboration. Second, and in the same spirit of transparency, ELTE has not previously hosted a funded MSCA fellow (this is recorded as an operator-declared assumption, not as evidence), and the institute's detailed recent-project, publication and doctoral-supervision record is a host-capacity item that only the participating organisation can supply; it is therefore developed in Part B-1 §3.2 rather than asserted here, so that the evaluator can see where the confirmed supervision arrangements end and the host-capacity detail begins.

## 1.3.2 Planned training activities for the researcher

Training is structured around a Career Development Plan (deliverable D1.3, Career Development Plan, due month 3), established jointly by the supervisors and the researcher and signed by both supervisors and the fellow — the joint establishment the call mandates, read as "both supervisors" because a co-supervisor is in place. The plan is agreed early in the action and reviewed at five governance points (M6, M12, M16, M20 and M27), the M27 review falling inside the placement window precisely so that non-academic career development is monitored when it is most in play. The plan spans research objectives (O1–O6), training and career needs, transferable skills, teaching, publications planning and open-science engagement, and it is the instrument through which the three training strands below are sequenced and reviewed.

**Scientific and technical training (host → fellow).** The host delivers eleven target competences as supervised research practice embedded across WP2–WP5 plus named ELTE courses: geoinformatics; EO time-series analysis; optical/SAR integration; hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer; spatio-temporal modelling; Bayesian hierarchical modelling; uncertainty quantification; transfer learning/domain adaptation; reproducible geospatial computation; research software/web deployment; and IP and research exploitation. These map directly onto the fellow's stated competence gap (Bayesian/probabilistic modelling, spatio-temporal AI, sensor-domain transfer, uncertainty, cross-country adaptation and decision evaluation) and onto the intended progression from Plant Physiologist/Agronomist to EO/Geospatial Crop Scientist to an independent researcher in transferable agricultural intelligence.

**Transferable and management skills.** Seven transferable-skill strands are trained: research integrity; open science and FAIR practice; generative-AI literacy; grant writing; IP and exploitation; project management; and science communication. This satisfies the call's requirement (SR-04) that training integrate key transferable skills — expressly including digital skills such as generative AI — and foster an Open Science culture, knowledge valorisation and good scientific conduct including research integrity. Management competence is trained concretely rather than nominally: the fellow runs the work plan, keeps a monthly written progress record, and sits in the Project Steering Group, gaining first-hand project-management and coordination experience across an academic–research–industry consortium.

**Teaching and education.** Two teaching measures feed research results back into host teaching: co-designing and delivering a full module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture (rather than a single guest lecture), and co-supervising the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work. In the Career Development Plan the teaching component is framed not as a competence to be acquired but as an existing strength — five years of syllabus design, lecturing and examining at Agricultural University Plovdiv (2015–2020) in Bulgarian and English, with Bachelor's thesis supervision — transferred to a new discipline, a new institution and a new language of instruction, and stepped up from Bachelor's to doctoral-level supervision.

**Publications and public engagement.** The plan targets four principal scientific outputs (P1–P4) with at least two high-quality peer-reviewed submissions during or shortly after the fellowship, one public field demonstration with AgroVIR farmers, and one public-facing article per year. This supervision-and-training design cadences the fellow's development: a weekly one-to-one with the supervisor, a weekly technical session with the co-supervisor through WP3 and WP4 (M6–M21) tapering to monthly outside that window, a monthly written progress record, and a quarterly review against the Career Development Plan attended by both supervisors.

## 1.3.3 Two-way transfer of knowledge between researcher and host

The transfer of knowledge is genuinely bidirectional, and it is constitutive of the science rather than a courtesy: the physiological target defines what the geospatial model must predict, and the geospatial-modelling apparatus determines which physiological signatures can be scaled and forecast. From host to fellow, ELTE transfers the eleven geospatial and data-science competences listed in §1.3.2. From fellow to host, Dr. Rositsa Cholakova brings the plant-science foundation the host's remote-sensing and meteorology groups do not themselves hold: plant physiology; horticultural crop science; plant protection/agronomy; water-stress experimentation; physiological phenotyping; hyperspectral field measurements; biological interpretation of Earth-observation signals; the preliminary development of the DrR - Digital Agronomist prototype; and access to complementary agricultural research collaborations. The net exchange is crop physiology/agronomy ↔ geospatial/data science — the two disciplinary bases that §1.2 integrates into a single method — and it directly serves the call's expected outcomes on stronger R&I capacity and better knowledge transfer among participating organisations (EO-07) and on enhanced quality and sustainability of research training and supervision at the host (EO-05).

Although the formal European-Fellowship requirement concerns the researcher and the host only, the associated partners enrich this exchange into an academic–research–industry knowledge chain without altering where the two-way obligation sits. Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem (MATE) contributes long-term experimental and physiological knowledge and the source-domain dataset for model development and validation; Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив (MVCRI) contributes the independent Bulgarian research environment for the Hungary→Bulgaria cross-country transferability test (a true geographic transfer, not merely a larger sample); and AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság contributes the bridge from research field to farmer field and from research prototype to operational requirements. The fellow is the connective tissue of this chain, carrying physiological understanding into a geoinformatics faculty and geospatial-prediction competence back out toward operational agriculture.

## 1.3.4 Rationale and added value of the non-academic placement

The action includes an optional non-academic sector placement, permitted under the call (SR-06) as up to six additional months at the end of the fellowship in a non-academic organisation established in an EU Member State, and required to be an integral, explicitly justified and evaluated part of the proposal. AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság (a private for-profit SME in Budaörs, Hungary, operating a commercial farm management information system used across more than 745,000 hectares in eight countries, including Hungary and Bulgaria) hosts the placement over the final six months of the 30-month action (M25–M30). The company co-leads WP5 (Operational Transfer, Decision Value and Web MVP) from earlier in the action and then hosts the fellow on site, so the placement deepens existing WP5 content rather than introducing a new strand.

**Added value for the project.** The placement makes the operational-transfer half of the proposal structural rather than asserted. Gap G5 and hypothesis H5 both claim that research-to-farm transfer is where locally developed agricultural models break; a six-month period embedded inside the company that runs the farms is the strongest available evidence that the proposal takes its own thesis seriously, and it directly answers the previous evaluation's recorded criticism that the economic and technological route to users was insufficiently substantiated. **Added value for the researcher's career.** The placement supplies the inter-sectoral half of the intended career progression — operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation and direct exposure to commercial agricultural-software requirements — none of which the academic host can provide, and it is the segment of the profile that makes the fellow employable in precision-agriculture, irrigation-technology and FMIS companies as well as in academia. **Why it must be inside the company and why it needs six months.** The concrete work content of the placement depends on the company's own production environment and its customer-facing requirements: operational hardening of the prediction pipeline in a production FMIS environment; the nine-dimension operational assessment producing D5.4 (AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation, due month 30); the FMIS integration roadmap written from inside the implementing company, producing D5.5 (FMIS integration roadmap, due month 30); and requirements engineering and user testing with commercial growers. So that the placement is validation and transfer rather than first build, the web MVP is delivered before the placement begins as D5.1 (DrR web MVP, due month 24). The fellow is supervised on site by Miklós Maróti, senior research officer at the company — a research-grade supervisory register appropriate to the placement's training rationale — with a working desk/office location and access to the company's FMIS development/staging and customer-data environments for the six months; these on-site hosting facts rest on operator declarations about AgroVIR's own staff and facilities and are recorded as assumptions to be confirmed with the company, in line with the honest sourcing applied throughout this proposal. In accordance with the Guide for Applicants, the placement is described here in Part B-1 for assessment under this criterion, no letter of commitment is included for the non-academic placement host, and the six-month ceiling is used in full.

sub_sections.title: Quality and appropriateness of the researcher's professional experience, competences and skills
sub_sections.content:
## 1.4 Quality and appropriateness of the researcher's professional experience, competences and skills

### 1.4.1 An experienced researcher whose profile is matched to a training-through-research action

FIELDWISE is carried out by the experienced researcher Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, who holds a doctorate and therefore meets the MSCA-PF experienced-researcher condition. Her professional experience is appropriate to this fellowship in a specific and demanding sense: MSCA-PF is a training-through-research action, so the relevant test is not that the researcher already possesses every competence the project requires, but that her existing experience is strong exactly where the project's scientific object is anchored, is genuinely complementary to what the host adds, and defines a coherent development trajectory. On all three counts her profile fits the action. Her established strength is the biological, physiological and agronomic half of the project — precisely the half that the host's remote-sensing and geoinformatics groups do not themselves hold — while the geospatial, uncertainty-aware modelling half is the deliberate, structured gap the fellowship is designed to close (see §1.3). Her professional experience is therefore not merely adequate but load-bearing for the interdisciplinary integration that §1.2 identifies as constitutive of the objectives O1–O6.

### 1.4.2 Depth in the project's core discipline: plant physiology, agronomy and the model crop

The scientific core of FIELDWISE — a physiologically meaningful definition of crop water stress in processing tomato, observed through soil, meteorological and hyperspectral data — sits squarely within Dr. Cholakova's trained expertise. She completed her PhD in Plant Physiology at Agricultural University – Plovdiv (doctoral studies 2014–2020, EQF level 8), with doctoral research in plant stress physiology (her thesis, an English rendering of the Bulgarian original, concerns the response of maize to low temperatures and the effectiveness of subsequent foliar fertilisation), supervised by Prof. Dr. Andon Vassilev. She has since held the post of Assistant Professor in Plant Physiology and Plant Stress Physiology at the same university (2015–2020) and is currently Chief Assistant Professor and plant physiology researcher at the Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute (from 15 October 2024). This is the disciplinary competence — plant physiology, horticultural crop science, plant protection/agronomy, water-stress experimentation, physiological phenotyping and hyperspectral field measurement — that she transfers to the host under the fellow→host direction of knowledge transfer, and it is what makes WP1 (Historical Data and Target Design) and WP2 (Physiological Early Warning and Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel Transfer) achievable: only a plant physiologist can define the physiological stress target the geospatial model must learn to predict.

Her current research directly concerns the FIELDWISE crop and the FIELDWISE stress. She works on project ZEMDKT 17 (2024–2026), whose Task 7 studies resistance to abiotic stress — drought and salinity — in Solanum lycopersicum, i.e. tomato under water and osmotic stress, and she participates in SolGenSys (2026–2030) on tomato multi-stress tolerance. Her experience is thus not adjacent to the project's biology; it is the same crop and the same physiological problem the fellowship addresses, which is the strongest available evidence that the researcher can execute the physiological programme rather than merely commission it.

### 1.4.3 An emerging, honestly-scoped Earth-observation and geospatial track record

The appropriateness argument is stated with candour rather than overstatement. The Earth-observation and geospatial side of Dr. Cholakova's profile is emerging, not yet consolidated: of her body of published work, only three items touch remote sensing, all dated 2025 or later and all with her as a middle author, so the EO half of her profile rests not on a publication record but on demonstrable, hands-on engagement with geospatial method — namely a COST Action CA22136 (PANGEOS) Short-Term Scientific Mission hosted at MATE in Hungary in 2025; three Erasmus+ staff-mobility grants to MATE (Hungary) and the University of Novi Sad (Serbia) in 2025–2026; an Erasmus PhD mobility to the Timiryazev Academy in Moscow (2018); and an operational A1/A3 UAV pilot licence issued by the Civil Aviation Administration of Bulgaria. She is a member of three COST Actions (CA22136 PANGEOS, CA22149 AI4Insect and CA22141 REcrop) and participates in KP-06-COST/2 (2025–ongoing), which monitors vegetable crops for precision agriculture using satellite and unmanned aerial systems together with the Space Research and Technology Institute of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences. She has also begun the transition formally, undertaking a second MSc in Environmental Engineering (2025–2026), and has already built preliminary technical capacity by initiating the DrR - Digital Agronomist prototype that integrates soil-sensor, field-meteorological and Sentinel-2 data. Presenting this evidence as a credible but incomplete geospatial foundation — rather than claiming a finished EO scientist's CV — is what makes the fellowship's training rationale honest: there is a real gap in Bayesian/probabilistic modelling, spatio-temporal AI, sensor-domain transfer, uncertainty quantification, cross-country adaptation and decision evaluation, and FIELDWISE is designed to close it.

### 1.4.4 Transferable competences: teaching, inter-sectoral exposure and proposal maturity

Beyond the two scientific halves, the researcher brings transferable competences that materially strengthen the action. She has five years of university teaching at Agricultural University – Plovdiv (2015–2020), including syllabus design, lecturing and examining in both Bulgarian and English (including for Erasmus students) and the supervision of Bachelor's theses, together with specialist advisory work for farmers on physiological monitoring and integrated plant protection. This is why the fellowship's teaching component (§1.3) is framed as an existing strength transferred to a new discipline, a new institution and a new language of instruction, rather than a competence to be acquired — a direct contribution to the call's expected outcome on feeding research results back into teaching (EO-08). She additionally holds recent non-academic experience as a Data Analyst at KPMG Global Hungary (2024) and earlier as an agricultural market analyst, giving her prior exposure both to data-analytic practice and to a commercial working environment — relevant preparation for the operational, decision-value and non-academic-placement components of WP5 (Operational Transfer, Decision Value and Web MVP). Finally, the researcher has already carried a closely related concept through the full MSCA-PF process: the predecessor application PLANTDIGISENSE (HORIZON-MSCA-2025-PF, proposal 101284764), with the same host, scored 70.40% against a 70.00 threshold, demonstrating that she can design and articulate a fundable research programme at this level. FIELDWISE is a strengthened resubmission by a researcher who has already reached the threshold, not an untested first attempt.

### 1.4.5 Prior familiarity with the host environment and the intended career trajectory

Dr. Cholakova's experience is also appropriate to this particular host and this particular mobility. Her documented mobilities have repeatedly brought her into the Hungarian research environment and, specifically, into contact with the host and its partners — a PANGEOS STSM and Erasmus+ staff mobilities at MATE, an Erasmus master's mobility internship at ELTE in 2026, and a period of professional activity in Budapest — so she arrives already familiar with the host country, the partner MATE that supplies the source-domain dataset, and the host institution itself. This lowers the integration risk of the fellowship and reinforces the two-way transfer described in §1.3. Her experience maps onto a clear and realistic career progression: from Plant Physiologist/Agronomist, through EO/Geospatial Crop Scientist, to an independent researcher in transferable agricultural intelligence. The fellowship supplies exactly the missing segment of that trajectory — advanced competence in Bayesian/probabilistic modelling, uncertainty quantification, spatio-temporal validation, sensor-domain transfer, cross-country adaptation, operational AI evaluation and research-to-MVP translation — and the experience she already holds is what makes that acquisition credible within 30 months. In accordance with the call, her intervening career break (full-time parenting, July 2021–May 2024) is declared in Part A and does not count against the experienced-researcher time ceiling, so it does not diminish the appropriateness of her research experience. The result is a researcher whose existing professional experience is deep where the science is anchored, honestly emerging where the fellowship trains, and directly aligned with the call's expected outcomes on increased research and transferable skills and improved employability (EO-01) and on new inter-sectoral, interdisciplinary mind-sets (EO-02). Note on identity: the researcher publishes her pre-2020 work under the name Rositsa Cholakova-Bimbalova and her later work under Rositsa Cholakova; both name forms denote the same person and both are carried in Part A so that the full record attaches to the applicant.
